claim.description: The core capabilities this plugin claims, and the probes each is shown by.

contribution.description: The rows it adds at the points lemonfiber publishes.

override.description: Every bundled thing it will change.

plugin.description: Who the plugin is, and where it came from.

proof.description: What must hold before it is installed.

recipe.description: The ordered calls that configure what it installed.

requires.description: What the plugin needs of lemonfiber.

service.description:
What runs. One or more.

More than one because a plugin is often a thing and the thing beside it: Plex
and the reader of its watch history are one install and one uninstall to an
operator, and are two containers on two tiers with two criticalities. A format
permitting one forces the author of the pair to choose the wider tier for both
halves, or to publish two plugins an operator has to keep in step by hand.

wiring.description: How the stack's own proxy and dashboard reach its services. One each, at most.

Capture.description: A value taken out of an answer.

from.description: Where in the answer it is read from.

name.description: What the value is called, for a later call to name.

Claim.description:
The core capability a plugin claims, and the probes it is demonstrated by.

The vocabulary owns what must be shown; this owns where to ask. A capability is
one contract with many claimants, each answering at a path of its own, so the
published probe declares the question and the statuses that answer it, and the
binding declares the method, the path and the recorded response.

capability.description: A core name, which must also appear in the service's `provides`.

probe.description: One binding per probe the capability declares. Every one of them, exactly once.

ClaimProbe.description: One probe of a claimed capability, bound to a request on this plugin's service.

expect.description: What the answer must be, within what the probe permits.

fixture.description:
The recorded response.

Required here where it is optional on a proof: a claim nobody can demonstrate
without owning the service is a claim the catalogue's own checks cannot make.

id.description: Names a probe the capability declares.

request.description: Method and path on this plugin's own service.

Contribution.description:
A row in a register lemonfiber already runs.

The fields beyond `at` and `id` are the row its point declares, and the point is
published — so the required set, the optional set, the closed sets and the bounds
are read from `extension-points.json` rather than restated here. What this type
fixes is that a contribution is declared in this block and nowhere else, and that
it carries nothing outside the union of the rows the published points take.

action.description: What to do, in the imperative.

at.description: A point the build publishes. One it does not is refused by name.

category.description: Which family a check is narrowed to.

detail.description: The technical half of a remedy, which must not lead.

fixture.description: The recorded response the check is proved against.

for.description: The check a remedy is for, which must be one this same plugin declared.

id.description: Namespaced with the declaring plugin's id, always.

request.description:
Method and path on the plugin's own service.

There is no field for a host, so a check cannot be pointed at another service,
at the machine, or off it. A plugin wanting to say something about a service it
did not install is asking to speak for somebody else's software.

service.description: Which service the finding is about. Defaults to the plugin's own.

timeout_s.description: How long a check may run, within the bounds the point declares.

title.description: The one-line summary of what was checked.

Expect.description:
What the answer has to be.

A status is a claim about the network path rather than about the service: Docker
publishes a port by putting a proxy in front of it, and that proxy accepts a
connection before knowing whether anything inside is listening. So a status alone
is not evidence — except for a refusal, which is the one answer no port proxy can
produce.

**A key of the four key-wise constraints is a place rather than a name.** A plain
name is a top-level member, and one beginning with `/` is a JSON Pointer, extended
with a step that picks an entry of a list by a field it holds. A flat name was enough while every service answered a flat object, and the
only thing it could say about a service that nests its payload was that the envelope
was there — which is a probe that passes by observing that something replied.

body_starts_with.description: What the body must begin with, where it is not JSON.

content_type.description: A substring of the content type the answer was served as.

json.description: Places the answer must carry, each with the exact value it must hold.

json_array_min.description:
The answer read as an array, with at least this many entries.

A catalogue is very often a list rather than an object, and none of the
object-shaped constraints can say anything about one.

json_at_least.description: Places the answer must carry, each with a number it must not be below.

json_has_keys.description: Places the answer must carry, whatever they hold.

json_is_absent.description:
The answer did not parse as JSON at all.

Which is what a service that serves its application shell for every path it does
not implement answers — and the reason a status alone proves nothing against
one: the shell comes back `200` whether the API behind it exists or not, so what
has to be said is that the body was *not* a document.

json_types.description: Places the answer must carry, each with the kind of value it must be.

status.description: The status the answer must carry.

Expected.description:
Exactly what a place must hold.

Three kinds and no nesting: a flag that must be set, a number that must match, or a
word. A value deeper than this is asking about a document rather than about a claim
— and where the thing worth asserting is deeper *in* the answer, the key reaches it
rather than the value growing to match.

ExpectedKind.description:
The kind of value a key must hold.

Five, and closed. A name outside them is one no runner could evaluate, and an
assertion nothing evaluates is a proof that silently checks less than it says —
which is worse than one that fails.

Named for what it is the kind *of*, rather than `Kind`, because this is published
and whoever generates from it flattens every definition into one scope. `Kind` is
the one name there a generator is certain to want for itself: every envelope this
contract describes is keyed by its `kind`, so the union of them is a `Kind` too, and
two of them in one module is a definition nothing can be compiled against.

Override.description: A bundled thing the plugin will change.

Pair.description: One value, and the one destination it may reach.

value.description: The captured value, by the name the capture gave it.

Plugin.description: Who the plugin is, and where it came from.

id.description: Unique, lowercase. The name it is installed and journalled under.

license.description:
SPDX identifier.

Recorded and shown rather than constrained. The bundled set is a curated list
this project stands behind and is OSI-licensed throughout; a plugin is the
operator's own choice, and refusing to install proprietary software on somebody
else's machine would be the tool standing between an operator and their stack.
A plugin whose licence is absent is refused; one whose licence is merely not
open is installed and said so.

upstream.description: Project URL, so the operator can judge the thing rather than the wrapper.

version.description: Semver. The plugin's own content version, moved by its author.

PluginBind.description:
Which tier a plugin's port is published on.

A tier, not an address. lemonfiber renders it to an address exactly as it does for
a bundled service, so the two-tier policy stays a property of the system rather
than a request the plugin makes.

PluginCriticality.description:
How much a plugin's service costs when it is absent.

Four rather than the stack's five. `critical` means *its failure has consequences
outside the machine*, and in the bundled stack exactly one service holds it; it is
not a severity a contributor assigns to their own work, because the classification
drives how failures are reported and how hard lemonfiber tries to stop the operator
proceeding. A manifest declaring it is refused by name, with these four listed.

oneOf.description: The form does not work without it.

PluginHealth.description: How to tell a plugin's service has started.

kind.description: Which kind of probe to use.

timeout_s.description: How long to wait before calling it unhealthy.

PluginHealthKind.description: The kinds of health probe a plugin's service can declare.

oneOf.description: Fetch a path on the service's port.
Open a connection to the service's port.
Trust the container's own reported state.

PluginRequest.description:
What is asked, and where.

Three fields and no more, and the third is the one worth explaining. A service that
answers XML unless a caller asks for JSON cannot satisfy a capability whose probe
requires a JSON assertion, and until this field there was nowhere to ask: Plex
answers `text/xml` at every path, including the one its health probe uses, unless
the request carries `Accept: application/json`.

**It is one media type and not a header map, and the difference is the point.** A
probe declares who it is asked as, and `none` on every `guarded` probe has meant what
it says partly because nothing could be presented. A map of headers would make that a
convention a reviewer has to hold — any service may name its credential header
whatever it likes, so no list of refused names could ever be closed — where one named
field keeps it a property of the format. A probe still cannot present anything,
because there is nowhere to write it.

accept.description:
The one representation the answer is asked for, as a media type.

Absent where the service needs no asking, which is most of them.

path.description: The path on the service being asked.

PluginService.description:
What runs.

Declared in the stack manifest's service vocabulary, restricted to these fields.
The restriction is the substance of it: the set of fields *is* the set of things a
plugin may ask for, so "what can this plugin reach" is answerable from the format
rather than from the instance.

bind.description: Which tier the port is published on.

config_path.description:
Where inside the container the one configuration directory is mounted.

`/config` is a LinuxServer.io convention rather than a standard, and assuming
it made a whole class of image uninstallable: a plugin whose image reads its
configuration somewhere else would be generated a container mounting a
directory the application never reads, passing its health probe and losing
everything it had written the moment the container was replaced.

The target is data; the source is still lemonfiber's, and there is still
exactly one of it.

digest.description:
`sha256:…`. What actually runs.

A tag is not a pin: it is a name the publisher can repoint, so the image
reviewed and the image run can differ with nothing in the manifest changing.
The digest is what lemonfiber writes into the generated entry.

health.description: How to tell the service has actually started.

id.description: Unique across the stack **and** every installed plugin.

image.description: Registry path, without tag or digest.

media_types.description: Which media types it handles, in the stack manifest's vocabulary.

port.description: Primary UI or API port, absent for a service with no listener.

provides.description:
The capabilities this service claims.

A core name comes from the published vocabulary and means the contracted thing
that vocabulary defines; a plugin's own must be namespaced with the plugin's id
and is inert until something asks for it.

tag.description:
The human-readable version the digest corresponds to. Recorded and shown;
never resolved.

takes_data.description: Whether it needs the data root mounted.

Proof.description: What must hold before a plugin is installed.

fixture.description: A recorded response to run against where no instance exists.

id.description: Unique within the plugin. What a verdict is reported against.

service.description:
Which of this plugin's services is asked.

Optional where the plugin declares one, required where it declares more. A proof
gates the install of every service the plugin brings, and one that did not say
which it was about would be checked against whichever the reader reached first —
including its digest, which is what ties a recording to the image it came out of.

title.description: What it establishes, in one line.

why.description:
Why this is worth asserting. A proof nobody can justify is one nobody will
maintain.

pair.description:
Every value this flow could carry to every destination it could reach.

A flow with no pair behind it fails validation before a call is made, which is
what makes "what does this plugin tell whom" answerable from the manifest.

step.description: The calls, in the order they are made.

title.description: What the flow accomplishes, in one line.

Requires.description:
What the plugin needs of lemonfiber.

Named capabilities and never a version. A plugin written a year ago against a
stack it has never met keeps working for exactly as long as the things it actually
uses still exist, and when it stops working the message says which thing went — a
version number cannot say that, because it conflates "older" with "missing
something you needed".

capabilities.description: What lemonfiber must offer for this plugin to be installable.

Secret.description:
A value the plugin will hold.

Declared before anything can capture one, because the rule is that a secret
captured but not declared fails validation — and a rule that cannot be stated for
want of a field is not being enforced.

id.description: What the value is, within the plugin.

capture.description: The values taken out of the answer, for a later call to substitute.

expect.description: What the answer must be for the flow to go on.

StepCall.description:
What one step calls.

`headers` and `body` are where an earlier capture is substituted, and they are the
whole of it. Without somewhere to put one, a recipe could name a destination and
capture a value and had no way to carry the one to the other — which is every
first-run flow there is: creating an account and reading back a token is worth
nothing if the token cannot then be presented.

They are also what makes the set of flows a recipe could produce computable by
reading it: every substitution inside a call is a flow from that value to that
call's destination, and a call with nowhere to substitute into produces none.

body.description: The body the call carries. A value may substitute an earlier capture.

headers.description: Headers the call carries. A value may substitute an earlier capture.

to.description: A service id in this stack, or a DNS name outside it. Never an address.

Wiring.description:
How the stack's own services reach a plugin's service.

The tier governs, not the plugin. Only a `lan` service is proxied, because the
bundled policy is that an admin surface does not get a hostname — and a plugin
that could publish its own address could put an admin surface on the household
network without touching anything the web-security checks inspect.

dashboard_group.description:
Which group on the bundled dashboard it appears under. Defaults to the group
the stack uses for its tier.

hostname.description:
The label in front of the operator's domain. A single DNS label — not a name,
an address or a port. Defaults to the service's id.

service.description:
Which of this plugin's services it is about.

Optional where the plugin declares one service, because there is nothing to
choose between; required where it declares more, because a hostname is a fact
about one service and a manifest that left it to be inferred would be inferring
which of two the household reaches.
